asthma_copd.title: Inhaled Corticosteroids and Sickle Cell Disease Severity in Adults Without Asthma: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
asthma_copd.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: People living with sickle cell disease (SCD) who have episodic cough and wheeze (ECW) without a diagnosis of asthma have high rates of pain episodes and acute chest syndrome. A previous trial, in which patients with SCD and ECW without asthma received 15 weeks of inhaled mometasone or placebo, showed that inhaled mometasone improved daily pain and reduced soluble vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1), a marker of disease severity in SCD.

OBJECTIVE: To examine the biologic effects and safety of long-term daily inhaled mometasone in patients without asthma but with SCD and ECW.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial recruited patients with SCD from December 2018 to May 2022. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either inhaled mometasone or placebo for 48 weeks. Data analyses followed the modified intention-to-treat principle and were performed between July and November 2023.

INTERVENTIONS: The inhaled mometasone group received 220 μg of inhaled mometasone furoate dry powder once daily. The placebo group received a matching placebo inhaler.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was percentage change in soluble VCAM-1 levels from baseline to end of study. Secondary outcomes included laboratory results, functional outcomes, patient-reported outcomes, and health care utilization.

RESULTS: Of the 77 patients who received the intervention and were included in the analysis, 40 were assigned to inhaled mometasone (mean [SD] age, 36.0 [11.6] years; 26 females [65%]) and 37 were assigned to placebo (mean [SD] age, 31.5 [8.6] years; 19 males [51%]). Compared with the placebo group, the inhaled mometasone group increased their soluble VCAM-1 levels by 42% (95% CI, -11% to 96%; P = .02). Point estimates for clinical outcomes favored the placebo group, although the findings were not statistically significant.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this trial of adults with SCD and ECW, extended courses of inhaled mometasone were associated with worsened markers of disease severity. Inhaled mometasone should not be used long-term in patients with SCD and ECW without a definitive diagnosis of asthma.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03758950.

asthma_copd.title: Elarekibep, an inhaled Anticalin protein, targets IL-4Rα locally: first-in-human randomized phase 1 trials of a novel potential therapeutic class in asthma.
asthma_copd.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elarekibep (AZD1402/PRS-060) is an Anticalin, a new class of inhaled therapeutic proteins, which has been engineered to inhibit interleukin-4 receptor α-subunit (IL-4Rα) signalling, a key target in asthma.

METHODS: Two phase 1 randomized, first-in-human, dose-escalating, single-blind studies (NCT03384290; NCT03574805) investigated single ascending doses (SADs) or multiple ascending doses (MADs) of elarekibep compared with placebo. In the SAD study, healthy participants received a single inhaled dose of elarekibep 0.1-160 mg, intravenous doses of 1 mg or 2 mg, or matched placebo. In the MAD study, participants with mild asthma and elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) received inhaled doses of elarekibep 0.2-60 mg or placebo twice daily for 10 or 17 days (single dose on day 10 in all but one cohort), continuously or intermittently.

RESULTS: In total, 148 participants were enrolled across both studies. No safety concerns were reported. Treatment-emergent adverse events were experienced by 34.7% (elarekibep, 35.2%; placebo, 33.3%) and 81.6% (elarekibep, 75.9%; placebo, 95.5%) of SAD and MAD study participants, respectively. Elarekibep was absorbed after inhalation, with dose-related increases in systemic exposure detectable with doses greater than or equal to 6 mg. In both studies, systemic exposure resulted in decreased levels of phosphorylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 6, a biomarker for systemic IL-4Rα target engagement. In the MAD study, rapid reductions of FeNO were demonstrated with doses greater than or equal to 2 mg, indicating pulmonary target engagement.

CONCLUSIONS: Elarekibep was well tolerated in both studies and demonstrated pulmonary and systemic target engagement. Elarekibep was investigated further in a phase 2a study (NCT04643158).

TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03384290. Registered 26 November 2017, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03384290 . NCT03574805. Registered 2 July 2018, https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT03574805 .

asthma_copd.title: Uncovering the heterogeneous effect of inhaled corticosteroids on COPD exacerbations with causal machine learning.
asthma_copd.abstract:
BACKGROUND: High blood eosinophil counts can predict an enhanced response to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), but additional insight in treatment effect heterogeneity is needed to optimize clinical disease management. We investigated if causal machine learning models can detect heterogeneity in the effect of two ICS-containing therapies on both time to first exacerbation and exacerbation rate, and if this approach can identify additional predictors of ICS response.

METHODS: Baseline characteristics from patients in the fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium/vilanterol (FF/U/V) and U/V arms of the InforMing the PAthway of COPD Treatment (IMPACT) trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02164513) were used to train a causal survival forest to estimate the effect of fluticasone furoate (an ICS) on time to first exacerbation for each patient. Similarly, a causal forest was trained for exacerbation rate. Results were averaged over 100 train and validation sets in a Monte-Carlo cross-validation approach. The analysis was repeated for a comparison of the FF/V and U/V arms.

RESULTS: This analysis included 4048 FF/U/V, 4034 FF/V and 2025 U/V patients. Significant p-values for AUTOC (area under the targeting operator characteristic) curve indicated that all models ranked patients well according to individualized treatment and that significant heterogeneity was detected in the effect of ICS on both exacerbation outcomes. Respiratory symptoms, reversibility of airflow limitation and lung function, in addition to eosinophils, were identified as important predictors by all models. The contribution of additional predictors in determining the effect of ICS was most apparent for patients at the lower end of the eosinophil spectrum.

CONCLUSIONS: This hypothesis-generating secondary analysis of IMPACT detected significant heterogeneity in the effect of ICS and indicated that, in addition to eosinophils, other clinical patient characteristics also contribute to the prediction of ICS response on both time to first exacerbation and exacerbation rate. The causal machine learning approach in this analysis can identify treatment effect predictors and patterns of response, to enhance insight in COPD disease phenotypes and heterogeneous treatment effects.

smoking_cessation.title: Combination bupropion-zonisamide facilitates rapid reduction in smoke exposure and prevents weight gain during switching to electronic nicotine delivery systems: A randomized clinical trial.
smoking_cessation.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: A pilot study suggested that the combination of bupropion (BUP) and zonisamide (ZON) could facilitate smoking reduction during switching to an electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS). This randomized controlled trial tested the hypothesis that BUP/ZON would produce greater smoking reduction than BUP alone or placebo (PLAC).

METHODS: Adults who smoked cigarettes, but were not seeking cessation treatment, were asked to switch to ENDS provided during study Weeks 1-12. Participants were randomized to receive BUP/ZON, BUP, or PLAC (N = 60 per group) during Weeks 2-8. Assessments included exhaled carbon monoxide (eCO), self-reported cigarette and ENDS use, dependence level, withdrawal symptoms, reward ratings, body weight, and adverse events. Outcomes were analyzed using modified intent-to-treat (mITT), complete-case, and per-protocol treatment-adherent samples (≥80% medication adherence).

RESULTS: The mITT analysis showed no treatment differences in end-of-treatment eCO but higher smoking abstinence rates in both active treatment groups than PLAC (26.7% BUP/ZON, 25.0% BUP, 10.0% PLAC). In the per-protocol sample, eCO was significantly lower with BUP/ZON than with BUP or PLAC. Early reductions in eCO during the first treatment week-more common with BUP/ZON-strongly predicted later outcomes. Exploratory complete-case analyses showed lower tobacco dependence and craving in BUP/ZON than control groups. Weight gain occurred in BUP and PLAC, whereas weight loss was observed in BUP/ZON.

CONCLUSIONS: Bupropion plus zonisamide shows promise for smoking reduction and cessation, particularly when medication adherence is maintained. Prevention of post-cessation weight gain may offer additional clinical and public health benefits. Larger trials with longer treatment duration are warranted.

smoking_cessation.title: A novel harm reduction approach for oncology outpatients who smoke and refuse traditional tobacco treatment: a protocol for a type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial.
smoking_cessation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Smoking rates are high among patients in cancer care, and improving quit rates among these patients is critical for improving survival outcomes. Yet, many oncology outpatients do not receive tobacco treatment, and a sizeable portion even refuse available evidence-based resources. E-cigarettes deliver lower levels of known carcinogens compared to cigarettes, and several rigorous trials have shown higher quit rates among people who receive e-cigarettes compared to those who receive nicotine replacement therapy. Switching from cigarettes to e-cigarettes reduces exposure to carcinogens and may be an appealing harm reduction intervention for patients in cancer care who refuse traditional treatment. The present protocol describes an ongoing type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial among oncology outpatients at an NCI-designated cancer center to compare rates of switching to e-cigarettes to standard care, and advance understanding of key barriers and facilitators of implementation processes.

METHODS: Adults who smoke cigarettes and refuse all components of traditional tobacco treatment through an opt-out tobacco treatment service are randomized to receive either (1) a 13-week supply of e-cigarettes and a workbook for switching to e-cigarettes or (2) a workbook for quitting smoking. Participants assigned to e-cigarettes are instructed to set a switch date within two weeks of randomization, to use their e-cigarette ad libitum in advance of their switch date, and to stop smoking cigarettes and exclusively use their e-cigarette on their switch date. Participants complete biweekly assessments through the end of product provision and additional follow ups through 6 months. The primary outcome is complete switching (7-day point prevalence abstinence confirmed by expired breath carbon monoxide ≤ 5ppm) at 6 Months. Secondary outcomes include implementation processes, biomarkers of cancer risk, and health-related quality of life.

DISCUSSION: This study examines a novel approach to harm reduction among oncology outpatients who refuse traditional tobacco treatment. Integrating effectiveness and implementation results helps to engage this population in harm reduction and provides critical evidence to refine delivery and planning for implementation. The proposed trial is highly significant, regardless of the results, and has the potential to influence harm-reduction approaches to tobacco use among patients in cancer care.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: The current study was registered on clinicaltrials.gov on June 26, 2025 (NCT07039292).

thai_herbs.title: Triple-pathway synergistic senolysis via AKAP1 silencing and calcium overload: An aptamer-functionalized DNAzyme nanoplatform for anti-pulmonary fibrosis research.
thai_herbs.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) lacks therapies that reverse disease progression, partly due to persistent senescent alveolar epithelial type II cells (SAEC II). We report a synergistic senolytic strategy combining mitochondrial calcium overload with AKAP1 silencing. An acid-responsive nanoplatform (CCMD@Lipo-Apt) comprising a CaCO3 core co-loaded with curcumin (CUR), Mn2+, and an AKAP1-targeting DNAzyme, enveloped by an L1CAM aptamer-modified lipid bilayer, enables SAEC II-specific homing. Upon lysosomal acidification, CaCO3 degrades to release Ca2+, CUR (mobilizing ER Ca2+), Mn2+, and the DNAzyme. Mn2+ simultaneously activates DNAzyme to knockdown AKAP1 (sensitizing mitochondria to calcium overload) and directly activates caspase-8. This triple mechanism collapses mitochondrial membrane potential and triggers robust apoptosis exclusively in SAEC II. In a bleomycin-induced mouse model, CCMD@Lipo-Apt clears SAEC II, attenuates fibrosis, and restores lung function without overt toxicity. This work establishes a synthetic-lethal axis for targeted IPF therapy.

thai_herbs.title: Integrated analytical characterization and multiscale modeling of supramolecular interactions in lumefantrine-curcumin coamorphous systems with enhanced biopharmaceutical and anticancer performance.
thai_herbs.abstract: Poor aqueous solubility, limited physical stability of amorphous forms, and suboptimal systemic absorption remains major challenges for lipophilic small molecule drugs. In this study, lumefantrine (LMF) and curcumin (CUR) were engineered into stoichiometry-controlled coamorphous systems (CAMS) using an interaction-driven solid-state design strategy. Integrated analytical characterization using powder X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, and attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the formation of homogeneous single-phase coamorphous matrices and established composition-dependent relationships between supramolecular organization, molecular mobility, and stability. Multiscale computational analyses integrating density functional theory, reduced density gradient analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations identified the dominant intermolecular interactions governing miscibility and stabilization within the CAMS. AI/ML models trained using interaction-derived molecular descriptors accurately predicted composition-dependent glass transition temperatures, showing close agreement with experimental measurements and simulation-derived estimates. Among the investigated systems, LC_12_CAM exhibited the most balanced supramolecular organization, integrating strong heteromolecular stabilization with controlled molecular mobility. This optimized architecture produced a ∼2-4-fold increase in apparent solubility relative to crystalline LMF and CUR and markedly improved dissolution performance, achieving >85-90% drug release within 6 h. The improved biopharmaceutical performance further translated into substantially enhanced systemic exposure of LMF in vivo and was accompanied by pronounced apoptosis-associated anticancer activity in A549 lung cancer cells. Accelerated stability studies confirmed sustained amorphous integrity of LC_12_CAM for six months, consistent with reduced moisture uptake observed in dynamic vapor sorption analysis. Collectively, these findings establish a stoichiometry-resolved structure-stability-performance framework for drug-drug CAMS and highlight the utility of integrated analytical characterization combined with multiscale predictive modeling for the rational design of stable, high-performing formulations of poorly soluble drugs.

cardio_renal.title: SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiorenal outcomes across operationally mapped cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome stages 2-3 and stage 4: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
cardio_renal.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reduce heart failure and kidney events across diverse cardiometabolic populations. The cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework offers a clinically relevant way to view these linked conditions, but randomized evidence has not been synthesized across this continuum. We assessed cardiorenal effects across two operationally mapped CKM stage groups.

METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and CENTRAL to February 25, 2026, for randomized controlled trials of an SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo or usual care. Trial populations or mutually exclusive published subgroups were categorized as CKM stages 2-3 or CKM stage 4. No single primary outcome was prespecified; five outcomes were registered as main outcomes, and all-cause mortality was registered as a secondary outcome. The six time-to-event outcomes were pooled using REML random-effects models. Prespecified sensitivity analyses examined model choice, exclusion of SOLOIST-WHF-whose selected efficacy result was judged at high risk of bias-kidney endpoint definitions, leave-one-out stability, and small-study effects.

RESULTS: Nineteen reports representing 11 parent randomized controlled trials (73,220 participants) were included: 18,547 in CKM stages 2-3 and 54,673 in CKM stage 4. Composite heart failure, hospitalization for heart failure, and kidney outcomes favored SGLT2 inhibitors in stages 2-3 and stage 4: HRs 0.80 (95% CI 0.68-0.93) and 0.77 (0.73-0.81; P for group difference = 0.65); 0.61 (0.48-0.77) and 0.71 (0.66-0.76; p = 0.24); and 0.61 (0.52-0.71) and 0.64 (0.54-0.75; p = 0.64), respectively. CKM stage 4 estimates for MACE and mortality were more precise. No group-difference test was significant. Sensitivity analyses were stable; an exploratory all-cause-mortality Egger test gave p = 0.025.

CONCLUSIONS: Heart failure and kidney estimates favored SGLT2 inhibitors in both groups. No statistically detectable between-group difference was observed; however, CKM stages 2-3 analyses relied on four estimates and were less precise, so the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent treatment effects.

cardio_renal.title: Influence of diabetes mellitus on dapagliflozin response after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR): insights from the DAPA-TAVI trial.
cardio_renal.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The DAPA-TAVI trial demonstrated that dapagliflozin reduced the composite of all-cause mortality or worsening heart failure (HF) at 1 year in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with prior HF. Whether the magnitude of this benefit differs according to diabetes mellitus (DM) status remains uncertain.

METHODS: This pre-specified subgroup analysis of the multicenter randomized DAPA-TAVI trial conducted at 39 centers in Spain, which enrolled 1222 patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR with prior HF and at least one high-risk condition. Patients were stratified by the presence or absence of DM. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality or worsening HF at 12 months. Secondary endpoints included the individual components of the primary endpoint, cardiovascular death, and safety outcomes. Cox proportional-hazards models adjusted for age, sex, coronary artery disease, baseline ejection fraction and baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate were used to estimate treatment effects.

RESULTS: Among 1222 patients, 537 (43.9%) had DM. In patients with DM, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the primary endpoint compared with standard care (15.2% vs. 22.7%; HR 0.580; 95% CI 0.389-0.866; p = 0.008; number needed to treat [NNT] = 11), driven primarily by fewer worsening HF events. In patients without DM, the reduction was numerically lower and non-significant (15.0% vs. 18.0%; HR 0.814; 95% CI 0.560-1.183; p = 0.280; NNT = 32). Genital infections were more frequent with dapagliflozin in patients with DM, whereas symptomatic hypotension was more common in those without DM. No significant differences in serious adverse events were observed in either subgroup. No statistically significant interactions between DM status and treatment effect were observed for the primary or secondary endpoints.

CONCLUSIONS: In this pre-specified subanalysis of the DAPA-TAVI trial, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the risk of death or worsening HF in patients with DM undergoing TAVR, with a favorable benefit-risk profile, whereas a more modest and non-significant effect was observed in non-DM patients. Although no statistically significant interaction according to diabetes status was observed, the apparently greater benefit among patients with DM warrants further investigation.

anticoagulation.title: Apixaban reduces hepatic decompensation in patients with cirrhosis (ApiHep): A randomized controlled trial.
anticoagulation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evolving data suggest that anticoagulation is safe in cirrhosis and may improve decompensation-free survival in select patients. This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of the direct oral anticoagulant apixaban in patients with cirrhosis.

METHODS: In this open-label randomized controlled trial with blinded endpoint assessment, adult patients (18-60y) with cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B7-C10) without splenoportal axis thrombosis were randomized (1:1) to receive apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) along with standard medical therapy (SMT) or SMT alone for 12 months. The primary outcome was the comparison of the proportion of patients with hepatic decompensation at 1 year. Secondary outcomes included frequency of liver-related events, overall and liver-related mortality, and adverse events (AEs).

RESULTS: One hundred thirty-four patients (mean age 43.4±9.5 y; Child-Pugh B/C:115/19) were randomized (67 Apixaban+SMT and 67 SMT). Patients receiving apixaban experienced significantly lower rates of hepatic decompensation compared with SMT (33.1% vs. 54.3%; absolute risk reduction 21.2% [95% CI: 4.5%-38.2%]; p=0.013). Although rates of ascites (6.4% vs. 17.4%), HE (21.2% vs. 36.0%), and variceal bleeding (7.5% vs. 14.6%) were lower among patients receiving Apixaban+SMT as compared with SMT alone, the differences were not statistically significant. No significant between-group differences in all-cause and liver-related mortality at 1 year were noted. There were no significant between-group differences in AEs (55.2% vs. 53.7%), any bleeding (41.8% vs. 46.3%), and major bleeding (9.0% vs. 11.9%) events.

CONCLUSIONS: Apixaban significantly reduced hepatic decompensation events without increasing hemorrhagic episodes in Child-Pugh B7-C10 cirrhosis (CTRI/2023/09/058018).

anticoagulation.title: Pharmacological strategies for hemodialysis arteriovenous fistula and graft patency: an access-stratified systematic review and network meta-analysis.
anticoagulation.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pharmacological therapies target different stages of hemodialysis access failure. We compared treatments separately in arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) and grafts (AVGs), accounting for differences in outcomes and follow-up.

METHODS: This PROSPERO-registered review (CRD420261411441) followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-NMA guidance. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL/Cochrane records, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through May 31, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed RoB 2. Separate random-effects frequentist network meta-analyses were supplemented by time-restricted analyses and exploratory follow-up meta-regression.

RESULTS: Among 1,557 records, 31 reports were included; 23 trial datasets contributed to the primary analyses (15 AVF and 8 AVG). In AVFs, ticlopidine (OR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.18-0.76) and clopidogrel (0.49; 0.24-0.97) may reduce predominantly early access failure (low certainty); estimates remained favorable at follow-up of 8 weeks or less. Larger single-trial effects for heparin plus anisodamine and clopidogrel plus a prostacyclin analog were very uncertain. Fish oil showed no clear AVF benefit. In AVGs, apixaban may reduce thrombosis (0.12; 0.03-0.41; low certainty), but its interval widened to 0.007-1.94 in the approximately 12-month subset. The aspirin estimate (3.35; 1.21-9.27) was very uncertain and imprecise under timing restrictions.

CONCLUSIONS: Ticlopidine and clopidogrel may reduce early AVF failure without established improvement in functional maturation. AVG apixaban findings require confirmation, and the effect of aspirin remains very uncertain. Interpretation depends on the clinical outcome, follow-up, and bleeding risk.

ams_rdu.title: Short- versus long-course antibiotic therapy in non-severe CAP in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
ams_rdu.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Optimizing antibiotic duration for pediatric community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) may reduce treatment burden and support antimicrobial stewardship. Although recent randomized trials and evidence syntheses have reported similar clinical outcomes with shorter antibiotic courses, the effect of treatment duration on adherence-an especially relevant consideration in children-has received comparatively limited systematic evaluation. We therefore aimed to compare treatment effectiveness, medication adherence, and antibiotic-related adverse events between short-course and conventional-duration antibiotic therapy for non-severe CAP in immunocompetent children. PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO Global Index Medicus were sought through April 25, 2025. Only randomized clinical trials that included immunocompetent children < 18 years with non-severe CAP and compared short-course (≤ 5 days) with longer therapy (> 5 days) were considered. Data extraction and risk of bias (ROB 2) assessment were performed by two independent reviewers. Summary data were extracted by published reports. The principal outcomes were treatment effectiveness, assessed through treatment failure and relapse according to the definitions prespecified by each trial, and medication non-adherence to the active (non-placebo) study drug. Antibiotic-related adverse events were assessed as a secondary outcome. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Two hundred thirty studies were originally screened, after removal of duplicates and 10 trials (n = 8970) met inclusion criteria. No significant differences were found in treatment failure [RR = 1.07 (95% CI, 0.93-1.24), I2 = 3%] or relapse [RR = 1.04 (95% CI, 0.72-1.49), I2 = 0%]. Shorter regimens markedly reduced non-adherence [RR = 0.35 (95% CI, 0.24-0.50), I2 = 54%], the most consistent and clinically meaningful difference. Adverse events were comparable [RR = 0.71 (95% CI, 0.36-1.40), I2 = 81%].

CONCLUSIONS: Short-course therapy was not associated with significantly different treatment failure or relapse rates compared with longer regimens and was associated with substantially lower non-adherence. These findings support shorter antibiotic courses as a reasonable treatment option for non-severe pediatric CAP, while acknowledging that the present meta-analysis was not designed to formally establish non-inferiority or equivalence.

WHAT IS KNOWN: • Short-course antibiotic therapy may achieve similar clinical outcomes to conventional longer courses in children with non-severe community-acquired pneumonia. • Medication adherence remains an important challenge in pediatric antibiotic therapy.

WHAT IS NEW: • This meta-analysis found no significant difference in treatment failure or relapse between short- and long-course therapy. • Short-course therapy was associated with substantially lower non-adherence, highlighting an important practical advantage of shorter regimens.

ams_rdu.title: Nafithromycin in community-acquired bacterial pneumonia: a focused systematic review of the human clinical development program.
ams_rdu.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nafithromycin is a novel lactone ketolide being developed as a short-course oral treatment for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP). Its clinical development program includes early pharmacokinetic studies in healthy adults and later-phase efficacy trials in patients with CABP. This systematic review aimed to synthesize the available human clinical evidence on its pharmacology, safety, and efficacy.

METHODS: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261367133). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Clinical Trials Registry - India were searched from inception to 12 April 2026. Clinical studies evaluating nafithromycin in humans at any stage of development were eligible. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Given heterogeneity in study phase, design, population, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively.

RESULTS: Four studies were included: two Phase 1 studies in healthy adults, one Phase 2 randomized comparative study, and one Phase 3 randomized non-inferiority trial in adults with CABP. Early-phase studies suggested that nafithromycin was generally well tolerated in the short term and had pharmacokinetic properties supportive of once-daily dosing, including high pulmonary exposure in epithelial lining fluid and alveolar macrophages. In the Phase 2 study, early clinical response rates were high with both 3-day and 5-day nafithromycin regimens. In the Phase 3 trial conducted in India, a 3-day oral nafithromycin regimen was non-inferior to 7-day moxifloxacin for early clinical response at Day 4, with no severe TEAEs, serious TEAEs, or deaths reported in either treatment arm. However, the evidence base remains limited in size and geographic diversity, and data in older adults, patients with renal or hepatic impairment, and microbiologically confirmed macrolide-resistant pneumococcal disease were sparse.

CONCLUSIONS: Nafithromycin is a short-course oral candidate for CABP with supportive early clinical and pharmacokinetic data, but the current evidence base remains limited. Further evidence is needed to clarify its generalisability, rare or delayed safety profile, and effectiveness in microbiologically confirmed macrolide-resistant pneumococcal disease.

deprescribing.title: Barriers and enablers to deprescribing from the perspectives of older adults with polypharmacy and their stakeholders: A systematic review of qualitative studies.
deprescribing.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The appropriateness of polypharmacy remains debated, with growing concern about the consequences of complex and potentially inappropriate medication use among older adults. Deprescribing is a complex process involving patient and caregiver engagement, clinician-patient communication, and shared decision-making. Understanding barriers and enablers to deprescribing may support shared decision-making and improve the implementation of deprescribing interventions and patient outcomes.

OBJECTIVE: To identify the barriers and enablers influencing deprescribing among older adults with polypharmacy and relevant stakeholders.

DESIGN: This was a systematic review of qualitative studies.

METHODS: Computerized searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL Complete, and PsycInfo. The search scope was limited to articles published from the inception of each database up to December 2025. The Joanna Briggs Institute criteria for qualitative research were utilized to evaluate the quality of the studies, and a thematic synthesis approach was employed to integrate the findings. The Theoretical Domain Framework was used to map barriers and enablers to deprescribing from the perspectives of older adults with polypharmacy and their stakeholders.

RESULTS: A total of 52 studies were included, revealing 18 barriers and 11 enablers across three overarching themes: patient-level factors; physician-patient relationship and communication factors; and healthcare professional-level factors. Attitudes toward medication discontinuation among older adults with polypharmacy are shaped over time by medication-related experiences and interactions with healthcare professionals. The physician-patient relationship can facilitate engagement in deprescribing, whereas inadequate communication may reinforce reliance on long-term medication use. Healthcare professionals also play key roles in initiating and implementing deprescribing. Subthemes were mapped to nine of the 14 domains of the Theoretical Domains Framework, with Social influences, Environmental context and resources, and Beliefs about consequences being the most frequently represented domains.

CONCLUSIONS: This review identified that attitudes toward deprescribing among older adults with polypharmacy are shaped by accumulated medication-related experiences and ongoing interactions with healthcare professionals. Effective physician-patient communication and the active involvement of healthcare professionals are important for facilitating deprescribing, while factors related to healthcare professionals may influence its initiation and implementation. Mapping to the Theoretical Domains Framework identified key behavioral domains that provide a theoretical basis for designing theory-informed interventions to support deprescribing. Together, these findings may inform the development of patient-centred strategies that facilitate safe and effective deprescribing among older adults.

STUDY REGISTRATION: The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251162311).

deprescribing.title: Cancer co-medication quality in older patients with polypharmacy: A large randomized trial testing a medication review versus usual care.
deprescribing.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) testing medication reviews in geriatric oncology is sparse.

METHODS: We conducted a single-blinded RCT in ten rehabilitation clinics across Germany. Patients with common cancers, aged ≥ 65 years, and polypharmacy (regularly ≥ five drugs) were randomly allocated in equal proportions to usual care or a comprehensive pharmacist-led medication review conducted with the validated Fit fOR The Aged (FORTA) list. The FORTA score is the sum of drugs classified as potentially inappropriate medication (PIM) (each two points), drug underuse (each one point), and drug overuse (each one point). Changes in the FORTA score and its subcomponents from rehabilitation admission to discharge were tested using the chi-square test or the Wilcoxon's rank-sum test.

FINDINGS: At admission, 66.1%, 94.6%, and 58.9% of 443 trial participants included in the intention-to-treat analysis were exposed to PIM, medication underuse, or overuse, respectively, and the median FORTA score was six. At discharge, participants of the intervention group (n = 234) had a statistically significant greater reduction in the mean FORTA score than the control group (n = 209): mean difference [95% confidence interval]: -3.7 [-4.2; -3.3] score points. Furthermore, the proportions of subjects with PIM, underuse, and overuse were statistically significantly reduced by the intervention by 41.3, 35.5, and 30.7 percentage points (all p < 0.001).

INTERPRETATION: The pharmacist-led intervention with the FORTA list substantially improved the medication quality of older cancer patients with polypharmacy in clinical practice. A reduction of four FORTA score points (rounded) translates, for example, to the withdrawal of two PIMs or four drugs labeled overuse.
